relevant_group_routes.relationship: The Age of… volumes (1962–1994) as a synthesis of “the capitalist world from 1789 to 1991”, praised by reviewers for range and analytical grasp and called “unashamedly Eurocentric” by Judt
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Mediated: the four volumes are unread. Guardian obituarists (2012, read in full): the series "distilled the history of the capitalist world from 1789 to 1991" and "were not conceived as a tetralogy". Judt (NYRB 1995, read in full): the trilogy's scheme "eventually became the “conventional” interpretation, now exposed to steady criticism and revision"; "though unashamedly Eurocentric, Eric Hobsbawm has a unique range" (his endnote 2 defends the European focus). Black (Historein 2003–4, p. 215): "authoritative and commanding overviews of international history from the 18th century to present". Anderson (LRB 2002) quotes Hobsbawm on Interesting Times as "world history shaping that experience". At the 2014 conference (Times Higher Education report) Mazower spoke of a "golden age of historical synthesis". Counterweights: Judt's Eurocentrism remark and the existing critiques by Guha and Chakrabarty (edges 979, 917).
